title: Backend Networking & Resource Management
goal: Trace HTTPS from Java to the wire, diagnose resource contention, and build a restart-safe payment status reconciler.

sourceGuide.title: Download the complete networking self-study guide

outcomes: Explain DNS, routing, TCP, TLS, HTTP, client implementations, and resource reuse as separate responsibilities
Diagnose certificate, timeout, pool, queue, and thread failures with evidence
Implement bounded, durable polling and a local fake-provider reconciliation capstone
studyGuidance: Suggested pace: eight weeks at four to six focused hours per week; adjust to your own pace.
Use Java 25 or a supported JDK; match library documentation to the versions you run.
Predict → observe → experiment → explain → implement → test. Keep Prediction, Observation, Explanation, and Open questions in notes.
For each unit record a manual 0–4 score in notes: Unfamiliar, Recognize, Explain, Apply, Teach. Move on at Apply (3) and revisit after the capstone.
Work independently for 15–30 minutes, ask for hints or reasoning review, then reimplement the important portion without the solution visible.
Use localhost, example.com, and services you own or are authorized to inspect. Capture only your own loopback lab traffic; exclude production credentials and payment payloads.
Never disable TLS or hostname verification. Keep trust changes in a dedicated development truststore.
Use the full guide download for exact shell commands, the proposed lab repository layout, and the complete reference shelf.
completionCriteria: Every foundation unit is explainable without notes and has a reproducible lab report
Capstone acceptance checks pass with bounded queues and observable resource lifecycles
Restart, duplicate, stale-work, and uncertain-provider cases preserve the declared invariants
Complete the written self-assessment and oral design review; revisit any score at or below 2

material.explanation: An HTTPS operation crosses several responsibilities: application code, a concrete client, DNS when needed, the operating system, transport, TLS, routing, and the remote application. Those responsibilities are not one strictly serial packet timeline. Reusing a connection can skip setup; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP. In Spring RestClient, retrieve() prepares a response specification; a terminal operation such as body(...) or toBodilessEntity() is needed to execute the request.

workedExample.scenario: A shared client requests a local HTTPS endpoint twice.
steps: The first operation may require resolution, transport setup, and TLS negotiation.
The reused connection can avoid setup, but both requests still need HTTP and business processing.

commonMistakes: A socket connection or transport acknowledgement does not prove a business operation completed.

material.explanation: DNS resolves names, routing selects paths, ports identify transport endpoints, and NAT can rewrite outbound addresses. Diagnose them separately: a resolved address does not prove a port is reachable, and a successful TCP connection does not prove TLS or HTTP is valid. Resolver caches, IPv4/IPv6 selection, and network configuration can make laptop and deployment observations differ.

The provider may observe the gateway public IP rather than the container private address.

material.explanation: TCP offers an ordered reliable byte stream, not message boundaries. Applications must frame their own messages and handle partial reads, orderly end-of-stream, resets, and timeouts. Its acknowledgements indicate transport progress, not application-level payment completion. Learn flow control, congestion control, teardown, and keepalive as different mechanisms.

workedExample.scenario: A logical UTF-8 message is split across several writes.
steps: The receiver reads a four-byte length, validates it, then reads exactly that payload length.
The reconstructed message remains correct regardless of packet and read boundaries.

commonMistakes: One sender write is not guaranteed to match one receiver read.

Use bounded length-prefixed framing and try-with-resources.
Compare clean close, timeout, and connection reset observations.

acceptanceCriteria: Large and split-write messages reconstruct reliably

material.explanation: TLS adds confidentiality, integrity, and authenticated peer identity over an underlying transport. Certificate-chain trust and hostname matching are separate requirements. A Java truststore may differ from a browser trust system. Diagnose controlled failures by inspecting the chain, validity, hostname, and configured trust source; never solve the exercise by trusting every certificate.

Transactions: JDBC connections may be held through the scope of a database transaction.
HTTP client: max total connections vs per-route constraints; HTTP/2 multiplexing changes the relationship between requests and connections.

material.explanation: Pools lend reusable resources; they are not schedulers or executors. A borrowed JDBC handle may retain a physical connection through a transaction, while HTTP resource behavior depends on the chosen client and protocol. Acquisition timeout differs from query or response timeout. Budget connections across replicas and leave headroom rather than assuming more capacity always improves throughput.

workedExample.scenario: Four replicas configure twelve JDBC connections each, with fifteen other connections needed.
steps: The configured capacity budget is 4 × 12 + 15 = 63.
Actual usage can be lower, and the database still requires operational headroom.

commonMistakes: Increasing Hikari capacity does not fix an outbound HTTP bottleneck and can overload the database.
guidedExercise: Use a two-connection Hikari pool and coordinate a third borrower.
Measure active, idle, pending, and acquisition timeout behavior.
Repeat saturation on a bounded local HTTP pool and compare which resource waits.
material.independentExercise: Redesign an eight-second provider call inside a database transaction into short local transactions with explicit recovery.
recallQuestions: What does close mean on a pooled JDBC handle?

acceptanceCriteria: Borrowing and returning are observable without resource leaks

material.explanation: Incoming request threads, background executors, schedulers, HTTP pools, and JDBC pools are separate capacities. Slow dependencies can fill one while others look healthy. Bound admission, queues, and downstream concurrency. Virtual threads reduce the cost of blocking tasks but do not create unlimited external connections or remove the need for backpressure.

workedExample.scenario: The provider becomes ten times slower while Hikari pending stays low.
steps: Tomcat workers and the outbound per-route capacity fill.
Increasing JDBC connections does not address that dependency bottleneck.

commonMistakes: Moving work to Async or virtual threads does not remove capacity limits or failure handling obligations.
guidedExercise: Build an adjustable slow local HTTP endpoint.
Send a bounded batch through an executor.
Compare fast service, slow service, and overload with explicit rejection.
material.independentExercise: Draw a dependency-capacity graph and use throughput, latency percentiles, queues, and connection evidence to locate saturation.
recallQuestions: Why is a larger thread pool not necessarily better?
What does Async change and leave unchanged?

Why do virtual threads still need downstream limits?

acceptanceCriteria: Queued and in-flight work remain bounded

topics.title: Polling, webhooks, scheduling and reconciliation
topics.description: Polling repeatedly asks for status; pooling reuses resources.
learningGoals: Due work survives restart and is discovered after downtime
Provider calls are bounded and occur outside long database transactions
Duplicate and stale processing cannot create harmful repeated effects
Only authoritative results justify terminal payment outcomes
concepts: Polling = repeated status inquiry; pooling = reusable connection management.
Short polling, long polling, database polling and reconciliation.
Webhook/notification as push; polling as verification/fallback.
@Scheduled(fixedRate), fixedDelay, cron, and their actual scheduling behavior.
A scheduler determines when work runs; workers determine how much runs concurrently.
Persistent work state: next_check_at, attempt_count, status, last_error, locked_until/lease details when needed.
Terminal states, provider-defined expiry, retries, capped exponential backoff with jitter.
At-least-once processing, idempotent status updates, duplicate notifications, race conditions.
Safe coordination across replicas (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED transaction claiming, leases, or durable messaging). Lock only while claiming; do not hold a DB transaction open during external calls.
Reconciliation and uncertain outcomes: a failed inquiry does not imply payment failure.
examples: A payment is created at 10:00 with next_check_at=10:15.

Answer the recall questions without notes

material.explanation: Polling repeatedly asks for status; pooling reuses resources. Store per-payment due timestamps so restart does not erase scheduling intent. A scheduler discovers due work and bounded workers execute it. Claim work briefly, perform external I/O outside database transactions, and reconcile results with idempotent state changes and safe handling of stale or duplicate responses.

workedExample.scenario: A payment is created at 10:00 with next_check_at=10:15.
steps: The app is down at 10:15 and returns at 10:18.
The worker discovers the overdue persisted row rather than waiting for an app-start-relative timer.

commonMistakes: A timeout is uncertainty, not authoritative payment failure; neither a webhook nor a stale poll should blindly overwrite a newer terminal state.
guidedExercise: Define due-work schema and authoritative terminal states.
Separate claim, network call, and result-persistence steps.
Trace concurrent webhook, poll, retry, and process-restart cases.
material.independentExercise: Design a two-instance claim or lease policy with fencing or equivalent stale-result protection and idempotent business effects.
recallQuestions: Why is one sleeping thread per transaction a bad general design?
Should a webhook always win over a status-check response?
Why must status updates and business effects be idempotent?
When should the worker stop polling?

acceptanceCriteria: Due work survives restart and is discovered after downtime
Provider calls are bounded and occur outside long database transactions
Duplicate and stale processing cannot create harmful repeated effects
Only authoritative results justify terminal payment outcomes

material.explanation: This lab makes the Unit 2 mechanism observable instead of relying on terminology alone. TCP offers an ordered reliable byte stream, not message boundaries. Applications must frame their own messages and handle partial reads, orderly end-of-stream, resets, and timeouts. Its acknowledgements indicate transport progress, not application-level payment completion. Learn flow control, congestion control, teardown, and keepalive as different mechanisms.

material.explanation: Build two local services so every remote outcome can be controlled and observed. Persist creation intent, use a stable provider idempotency key, schedule per-payment due work, and separate brief database claims from network calls. A lease can expire while an old worker is still running: include stale-owner checks or fencing at result persistence, and make duplicated delivery harmless rather than promising impossible universal exactly-once execution.

steps: At 10:18 after downtime, a worker claims the persisted overdue row in a short transaction.
A timeout records uncertainty and a bounded next attempt without inventing a terminal outcome.
A later authoritative SUCCESS wins under the state policy and stops future checks; duplicate callbacks do not repeat effects.
